2.text: next year they crossed the Kolyma. They stopped at last just on the border of the western camps,

3.text: in the country of the Indighirka. It seemed almost as if they wanted to pass on to the land beyond

4.text: the Chukchee (i. e., to the Russian) territory. Only there they resolved to make a halt. So they

5.text: remained on the leeward (western) side. Ten years they spent in that country; and after many

6.text: years the ‘knowing men’ among the kinsmen of the murdered one made them (by magic) entirely

7.text: forget the past, and leave off their watchfulness. Then the youngest brother was murdered by means

8.text: of a spell from a great distance (by those ‘knowing men’).”

9.text: Then follows the episode of the spell. The youngest brother wounded

10.text: a wild reindeer-buck that came to his camp. While pursuing it on the ice

11.text: of the lake, he broke his own neck. Thus the reindeer proved to be a spell.

12.text: This part of the story has been mentioned elsewhere.¹ The narrator pointed

13.text: out that this man, one of the recent avengers, perished through an accident

14.text: connected with the shooting; and when dying had his bow in his hand, ready

15.text: to shoot. He had the same bow ten years before, when taking an active

16.text: part in their blood-revenge. Notwithstanding the incident of the spell, the

17.text: narrator, when speaking of the flight of the avengers westwards, added some

18.text: remarks of his own deprecating their lack of courage after the deed. His

20.text: “They fled without reason. Their deed was not a murder. Why have they left their own

21.text: country? They have only avenged their kinsman. And if they had staid there, they would have

22.text: met no annoyance, since they were only ‘exchangers.’ It is rather sinful to answer [the avengers]

23.text: with murder. Some such even live together, become friends and group-marriage companions; for

24.text: they may dwell in union, since they have accomplished their intention, as they would finish some

25.text: great work.² The others, however, may indeed feel afraid when the murderer has kinsmen who

26.text: are hot-tempered. Some also do not kill the murderer. They kill somebody else, a son or a

27.text: brother, or another man dear to his heart. They make the murderer suffer from sorrow. They

28.text: say, ‘You also suffer and repine.’ The man who has recently committed a murder feels the utmost

29.text: fear; but when retribution has been accomplished, he may cease to be afraid.”³

30.text: From all this the conclusion may be drawn that Chukchee blood-revenge

31.text: in most cases stops with the first case of retribution, and that the repaying

32.text: of revenge with further deeds of violence happens less frequently. On the

33.text: contrary, families having a feud, after the first act of revenge, may conclude

34.text: peace, and even form ties of friendship. I cannot say that I know of cases

35.text: of such friendship in actual life; but, on the other hand, the continuation of

36.text: blood-revenge through a series of return-cases does not correspond to the

37.text: general condition of Chukchee family life. The Chukchee family connection

38.text: is not strong enough to sustain a prolonged feud: at least, among the Rein-

40.text: ² A similar practice exists among the American Eskimo. Thus Franz Boas says about the Central Eskimo.

41.text: “Their method of carrying on such a feud is quite foreign to our fcelings. Strange as it may seem, a murderer

42.text: will go to visit the relatives of his victim, though he knows that they are allowed to kill him in revenge, and

43.text: will settle with them. He is kindly welcomed, and sometimes lives quietly for weeks and months. Then he

44.text: is suddenly challenged to a wrestling-match, and, if defeated, is killed: or, if victorious, be may kill one of

45.text: the opposite party; or when hunting, he is suddenly attacked by his companions and slain.” (Boas, Central

46.text: Eskimo, p. 582). All this may have place also among the Chukchee.
